sources.cite: NIMH, Ask Suicide-Screening Questions (ASQ) Toolkit, information sheet: four questions and a fifth acuity question asked after any yes; a yes to it is an acute positive, 'imminent risk', that needs a STAT safety and full mental health evaluation, and the patient 'cannot leave until evaluated for safety'; a non-acute positive needs a brief suicide safety assessment; refusing to answer counts as positive
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 in NIMH's PDF (summarizing fetch with short quotes). The four questions: a wish to be dead, feeling others would be better off, thoughts of suicide in the past week, any attempt ever. 'Clinical judgment can always override a negative screen.' Validated for youth and adult medical patients, including adult medical inpatients (Horowitz et al., Psychosomatics 2020); the toolkit has emergency department, inpatient and outpatient pathways (NIMH adult toolkit page, read the same day). The questions are paraphrased in the sim.

sources.cite: NIMH, Adult ASQ Toolkit: Brief Suicide Safety Assessment guides, nursing scripts and suicide risk screening pathways for the emergency department, the inpatient medical/surgical unit and outpatient primary care and specialty clinics
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 (summarizing fetch): an index page; the pathways themselves were not opened, so what each setting does after a positive screen is taken from the information sheet.

sources.cite: The Joint Commission, R3 Report Issue 18: National Patient Safety Goal for suicide prevention, NPSG.15.01.01 (effective 2019-07-01): EP1 environmental risk assessment; EP2 screen 'using a validated screening tool'; EP3 an assessment that 'directly asks about suicidal ideation, plan, intent, suicidal or self-harm behaviors'; EP4 document the risk level and the mitigation plan; EP5-EP7 policies for monitoring, discharge counseling and follow-up
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 (summarizing fetch with quotes; issue dated 2019-11-20, updated 2025-12-03). The report names one-to-one monitoring as a key protocol on nonpsychiatric units; it does not itself require it, so the observation level in each sim is the facility's policy.

sources.cite: The Columbia Lighthouse Project, Columbia Protocol (C-SSRS) triage page: 'the most worrisome answers are a recent (past month) yes to items 4 or 5' (intent, intent with a plan) 'and/or any recent (3 months) behavior'; next steps 'are setting specific', and 'interventions should be changed to reflect your individual resources and policies'
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 (summarizing fetch with quotes; page last modified 2024-03-22). The screener's items, relayed from the NCMHCE session (read 2026-11-11): wish to be dead; suicidal thoughts; thoughts with method; intent without plan; intent with plan; suicidal behavior.

brief.situation: Owen Ashby, 22 (a fictional client), was admitted yesterday to a medical unit for dehydration and weight loss. His roommate told admissions he has hardly slept in a week and has stopped going to class. At 15:00 you find him whispering to an empty corner. When you say his name he says, 'They keep telling me I should be dead.' He has no psychiatric history on file. His glucose and electrolytes this morning were normal; his temperature is normal. You are his registered nurse; you have about 30 minutes.
handover: Dehydration, improving on IV fluids; eating little; urine drug screen pending.
Unit policy: a positive suicide screen gets constant observation and a room check until the provider's brief suicide safety assessment.
howItWorks: Choose what to ask and how to respond from the action groups. Owen answers at once; then let the conversation continue, which moves the clock by the minutes that exchange took.
His trust, distress and how much he discloses change with what you say. Calm, simple, reality-based talk helps.
Your time ends at 30 minutes. Afterward you write a short formulation, then document the risk level and disposition.

source.note: About 30 minutes with one client on a medical unit (author's scenario timing).
How trust and distress move with each response is a teaching simplification for exam practice, not a validated model of a patient.

checkIn.label: Calm and simple: 'Owen, I'm your nurse. You seem scared. I'm here.'

effects.log: You sit at a comfortable distance and speak in short, calm sentences.

effects.finding: "You hear them too, right? They won't stop."

reflect.label: Reflect what you hear (empathic reflection)
reflect.why: You have reflected a lot already; move on.

effects.log: You reflect the feeling under what was said, without judging it.

effects.finding: He looks at you for the first time. "Yeah. Scared."

normalize.label: Present reality gently: 'I don't hear them, but I believe you hear them. That sounds frightening.'

effects.log: You say you do not hear the voices but believe he does, and that it sounds frightening.

effects.finding: "You believe me?" His shoulders drop a little.

screen.label: Screen with the NIMH Ask Suicide-Screening Questions (the four questions)
screen.why: He has answered; go on to the follow-up questions.

effects.log: You ask the four screening questions directly, in short, plain sentences.

then.finding: "Sometimes I wish I was. They say everyone would be better off. I've thought about it this week. Never tried."

then.log: Positive screen: a wish to be dead, feeling a burden, suicidal thoughts this week; no attempt.

then.finding: "I can't... they're too loud." (Too distracted to answer yet.)

argue.label: Tell him the voices aren't real and to ignore them

effects.log: You tell him the voices are not real and to ignore them.
Arguing with a hallucination breaks trust and does nothing for safety.

effects.finding: When you come back he is sitting on the floor, whispering.

You set his observation level.

formulation.question: Write your formulation for Owen: the signs of mental illness you saw, his risk and why, and what you put in place.

parts.label: Signs and risk
parts.criteria: Names signs of acute psychosis (auditory command hallucinations, responding to unseen stimuli, two weeks of no sleep, withdrawal, weight loss) and an acute positive screen with command hallucinations to end his life; oriented; substances to rule out; protective: his mother, roommate.
parts.modelAnswer: Signs of acute psychosis: auditory hallucinations he responds to, commanding him to end his life, after two weeks without sleep, with withdrawal and weight loss. He is oriented. The screen is an acute positive: thoughts right now when the voices are loud. Substances and medical causes still need ruling out. His mother and roommate are supports.

parts.label: What was put in place
parts.criteria: Names a calm, low-stimulation approach that accepts his experience without arguing, constant observation, a room check, the provider now with psychiatry, and the handoff.
parts.modelAnswer: Short, calm sentences; I said I did not hear the voices but believed he did; lights down and one voice; constant observation and a checked room; the provider called now for the safety assessment and urgent psychiatry; the charge nurse told and the handoff written.

safe.headline: Good: safe, with help on the way
safe.body: You recognized acute psychosis, met it calmly without arguing, screened, asked about command voices and put observation and the right people in place.

walkout.headline: The conversation broke
walkout.body: Telling him he is just tired dismisses what he is living through. Calm, simple, honest words keep him with you.

scoring.modelReasoning: Responding to unseen voices after weeks without sleep is a sign of acute psychosis. The nurse accepts the experience without agreeing with it, lowers stimulation and asks about command hallucinations and suicide directly. Command voices to end his life with thoughts right now make this an acute positive: constant observation, a room check, the provider now and psychiatry.
